title: SASSA Life Certification 2026: How to Complete Your Annual Verification Online
description: SASSA requires all grant beneficiaries to complete life certification annually. Learn how to verify using the new 2026 self-service portal, WhatsApp, or at a SASSA office.
imageAlt: Person using a tablet for online identity verification

steps.title: What Is Life Certification and Why Is It Required?
steps.content: Life certification is an annual process where SASSA confirms that grant beneficiaries are still alive and eligible. You must complete it once every 12 months to keep receiving your grant. Failure to complete life certification will result in your grant being suspended until you verify. In 2026, SASSA introduced a digital self-service portal that allows you to complete life certification online without visiting a SASSA office.
tips: SASSA will send you an SMS reminder when your life certification is due.
If your grant is suspended due to non-verification, it can be reinstated once you complete certification.

steps.title: Complete Life Certification Online (Self-Service Portal)
steps.content: The easiest method in 2026 is the SASSA self-service portal. Go to sassa.gov.za and look for the 'Life Certification' or 'e-Life Certification' section. You will need your 13-digit ID number and the cellphone number registered with SASSA. The system may ask you to complete a facial recognition scan (take a selfie) to confirm your identity. The entire process takes about 2 minutes.
tips: Make sure you have good lighting for the facial recognition scan.
The self-service portal is available 24/7 — complete it at any time.

steps.title: Complete Life Certification via WhatsApp
steps.content: The SASSA Self-Service WhatsApp (082 601 0111) includes review and proof-of-life checks. Send 'Hi', pick your grant type, and verify your identity with your mobile number and OTP. If SASSA has flagged your grant for a review, use the review/proof-of-life option to confirm your status instead of waiting for an SMS. If the WhatsApp self-service does not resolve it, complete the life certification on the official eLife portal or at a SASSA office.
tips: Save 082 601 0111 in your phone contacts to find it easily.
The WhatsApp method does not require facial recognition — you answer verification questions instead.

steps.title: Complete Life Certification at a SASSA Office
steps.content: If you do not have a smartphone or internet access, visit your nearest SASSA office in person. Bring your ID document and your SASSA card (Postbank Black Card or Gold Card). The SASSA officer will verify your identity and complete the life certification on their system. This option is available to all beneficiaries regardless of digital access.
tips: Go early in the morning (before 08:00) to avoid queues.
You can combine your life certification visit with other SASSA enquiries.

steps.title: What to Do If Your Grant Was Suspended
steps.content: If you missed the life certification deadline, your grant may be suspended. Do not panic — it can be reinstated. Complete the life certification using any of the methods above. Once the system confirms your verification, your grant will be reinstated and you will receive any back payments owed. Contact SASSA at 0800 60 10 11 if your grant is not reinstated within 14 days of completing certification.
tips: SASSA sends multiple SMS reminders before suspending a grant — check your messages regularly.
Reinstated grants are paid with back pay from the date of suspension.

faqs.q: How often do I need to complete SASSA life certification?
faqs.a: Once every 12 months. SASSA will send you an SMS reminder when your certification is due. You do not need to complete it more frequently.

faqs.q: Can a family member complete life certification on my behalf?
faqs.a: If you are too ill or frail to visit a SASSA office or use the online portal, a family member can arrange a SASSA home visit by calling 0800 60 10 11. The SASSA official will visit your home to complete the verification.

title: SASSA Grant Documents Checklist: What You Need for Every Grant Type 2026
description: Complete checklist of documents required for every SASSA grant. Print this list before visiting your SASSA office to avoid being turned away.
imageAlt: Checklist on a clipboard with a pen

steps.title: Documents Required for ALL Grant Types
steps.content: These documents are required for every SASSA grant application, regardless of which grant you are applying for: (1) Your 13-digit South African ID book or Smart ID card (original + copy). (2) Proof of residence — a utility bill, bank statement, or lease agreement dated within the last 3 months. (3) Your cellphone number (must be RICA-registered in your name). (4) Proof of income — payslips, bank statements, or an affidavit if you are unemployed. Have these ready before your appointment.
tips: Make copies of every document before going to the SASSA office — not all offices offer copying services.
Keep your original documents in a separate folder from copies to avoid losing them.

steps.title: Additional Documents for SRD R370 Grant
steps.content: The SRD grant is applied for online, so you do not need physical documents. However, you need: (1) Your 13-digit ID number (you do not need to upload the ID document). (2) A valid, active cellphone number registered in your name (for OTP verification). (3) Your banking details — bank name, account number, branch code. If you do not have a bank account, you can select Cash Send collection at Pick n Pay or Boxer.
tips: The SRD is the only SASSA grant that does not require any physical document submission.
Your banking details must match your ID exactly — a single digit error will delay payment.

steps.title: Additional Documents for Old Age Grant
steps.content: For the Old Age Pension (R2,400/month), bring: (1) Your 13-digit ID book or Smart ID card (original). (2) Proof of residence (utility bill in your name). (3) Proof of marital status (marriage certificate, divorce decree, or death certificate of spouse if applicable). (4) Proof of income and assets — pension statements, bank statements, property valuations. (5) Your spouse's ID copy if married (their income is included in the means test).
tips: Apply 3 months before your 60th birthday to avoid a payment gap.
If you are married, your spouse's income affects your eligibility — bring their documents too.

steps.title: Additional Documents for Disability Grant
steps.content: For the Disability Grant (R2,400/month), you need: (1) Your 13-digit ID document. (2) A medical assessment report from a government doctor (not a private doctor) confirming the disability. (3) Proof of residence. (4) Proof of income and assets. The medical report is the most critical document — without it, the application cannot proceed. The report must be dated within 3 months of your application.
tips: The medical assessment must be done at a government hospital or clinic — private doctor reports are not accepted.
If your disability is temporary (less than 6 months), apply for the SRD instead.

steps.title: Additional Documents for Child Support & Foster Child Grants
steps.content: For the Child Support Grant (R580/month per child): the child's birth certificate, your ID, proof of residence, proof of income. For the Foster Child Grant (R1,300/month): the child's birth certificate, the children's court order placing the child in your care, your ID, proof of residence, proof of income. The court order is mandatory for the Foster Child Grant — a letter from the child's parent is not sufficient.
tips: You can apply for the Child Support Grant while pregnant — the grant starts after the child is born.
The Foster Child Grant court order must be issued by a children's court, not a maintenance court.

steps.title: Documents Required for a Grant Review Appointment
steps.content: If SASSA has asked you to attend a grant review, bring these documents to your appointment: (1) Your original 13-digit South African ID book or Smart ID card. If you use alternative ID, bring your original refugee permit, asylum seeker document, or special permit. (2) Proof of residence — a utility bill, bank statement, or lease agreement dated within the last 3 months. (3) Your SASSA card (Postbank Black Card or old Gold Card) if you have it. (4) Proof of any income you receive — payslips if employed, pension statements, bank statements showing deposits, or an affidavit if you are unemployed. (5) Any documents SASSA specifically asked for in their SMS or letter. Bring original documents plus photocopies. Some SASSA offices offer copying services, but not all. For a full walkthrough of what happens during a grant review, see our [grant review and verification guide](/guides/grant-verification-process).
tips: Make photocopies of all documents before leaving home — keep originals in a safe folder.
If you were asked to bring a specific document and you do not have it, go anyway and explain — the officer may accept an alternative.
Call the SASSA office ahead of time to confirm which documents are needed for your specific review type.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring original documents or copies?
faqs.a: Bring both. SASSA staff need to see the original documents and will keep copies. Some SASSA offices offer copying services, but not all — make copies before you arrive.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a grant if I have lost my ID document?
faqs.a: No. You need your original ID book or Smart ID card to apply. If you lost your ID, apply for a replacement at the Department of Home Affairs first. This can take 2 to 8 weeks.

faqs.q: What documents do I need specifically for a grant review appointment?
faqs.a: You need your original South African ID (or alternative ID document), proof of residence dated within 3 months, your SASSA card if you have one, proof of income (payslips, bank statements, or an affidavit if unemployed), and any documents SASSA specifically asked for in their SMS or letter. Bring originals plus photocopies. See our [grant review and verification guide](/guides/grant-verification-process) for a full walkthrough of the review process.

title: SASSA Payment Methods 2026: Bank Transfer vs Postbank vs Cash Send vs Retail
description: Compare all SASSA payment methods: bank account deposit, Postbank Black Card, Cash Send at Pick n Pay/Boxer, and Post Office collection. Find the fastest and safest option.
imageAlt: Various payment methods: cash, card, and phone showing payment options

steps.title: Bank Account Deposit (Fastest & Safest)
steps.content: Having your SASSA grant paid directly into your bank account is the fastest and safest method. The money is deposited directly by SASSA into your account on your Pay Day date. You can withdraw it immediately without waiting for an SMS code or visiting a collection point. Your bank account must be registered in your own name — SASSA does not pay into third-party accounts. Major South African banks (Capitec, FNB, Standard Bank, Nedbank, Absa, Bank Zero, TymeBank, Discovery Bank) all accept SASSA deposits.
tips: Deposits usually reflect 2 to 3 business days after your pay date; Capitec and FNB often show them sooner.
Never close your bank account while waiting for a SASSA payment — it will cause delays.

steps.title: How Long Until Your Grant Reflects?
steps.content: Each payment method has a different reflection time after your assigned pay date. Bank account deposits usually take 2 to 3 business days. Postbank Black Card funds are normally loaded on the release date. Cash Send at Pick n Pay or Boxer is usually available the same day or the next business day once your SMS collection code arrives.
tips: Check your status page first to confirm your exact pay date before calling.
If nothing has reflected after 3 business days, call SASSA on 0800 60 10 11.

steps.title: Postbank Black Card (Formerly SASSA Gold Card)
steps.content: The Postbank Black Card replaced the old SASSA Gold Card in 2025/2026. If you do not have a personal bank account, SASSA will issue you a Postbank Black Card. Your grant is loaded onto this card and you can withdraw cash at any Post Office branch, any ATM (fees may apply), or participating retailers. The card is free and there are no monthly account fees. You can check your balance by dialing *120*3210# from any cellphone.
tips: Keep your PIN secret — never write it on the card or share it with anyone.
If your card is lost or stolen, call Postbank immediately at 0800 53 54 55 to block it.

steps.title: Cash Send at Pick n Pay or Boxer (No Bank Account Needed)
steps.content: Cash Send is a payment method for SRD grant recipients who do not have a bank account. SASSA sends a unique SMS code to your cellphone. You take this code to any Pick n Pay or Boxer store and the cashier gives you your R370 in cash. You do not need any card or bank account. The SMS code expires after a certain period, so collect your money promptly.
tips: The SMS code is unique to you — do not share it with anyone.
Cash Send is available only for the SRD R370 grant, not for permanent grants.

steps.title: Post Office Cash Collection
steps.content: You can collect your SASSA grant in cash at any South African Post Office branch. This method is available for all grant types. Bring your ID document and your SASSA card (Postbank Black Card). Post Office collection is free — no fees are charged. Post Office branches are open Monday to Friday 08:00 to 16:30 and Saturday 08:00 to 13:00. Avoid collection on the first few days of the month when queues are longest.
tips: Post Office branches are busiest on the first 3 working days of the month.
Some Post Office branches have limited cash availability — go early in the day.

steps.title: Comparing Payment Methods: Which Is Best for You?
steps.content: Choose the method that fits your situation: Bank account deposit is best if you have a bank account (fastest, safest, access your money anytime). Postbank Black Card is best if you do not have a bank account (free, works anywhere). Cash Send is best for SRD-only recipients without a bank account who live near a Pick n Pay or Boxer. Post Office collection is best for beneficiaries who prefer cash and live near a Post Office. You can switch methods by updating your payment choice on the SRD portal or at a SASSA office.
tips: You can change your payment method at any time — updates take effect the following month.
Bank deposit is strongly recommended if you can open a free savings account.

faqs.q: Can I switch from Cash Send to bank account?
faqs.a: Yes. Log into the SRD portal at srd.sassa.gov.za and update your banking details. The change will take effect from the following month's payment cycle.

faqs.q: How long does a SASSA bank transfer take?
faqs.a: Once your status shows 'Paid', the money usually reflects within 1 to 3 business days depending on your bank. Capitec and FNB are typically fastest.

faqs.q: Is there a fee for using the Postbank Black Card at ATMs?
faqs.a: Postbank ATMs are free. If you use other bank ATMs (Capitec, FNB, Absa, etc.), a withdrawal fee of approximately R2 to R8 may apply depending on the ATM owner.

title: How to Fix 'Bank Details Pending' on SASSA SRD in 2026
description: Your SRD status says 'Approved' but you see 'Bank Details Pending' and no payment has arrived. Follow this step-by-step guide to fix it and get your R370 paid.
imageAlt: Bank account and phone showing successful money transfer

steps.title: Understand What 'Bank Details Pending' Means
steps.content: When your SASSA SRD status shows 'Bank Details Pending', it means SASSA has approved your grant application for the month but cannot pay you because they do not have valid banking information linked to your application. Your money exists in the system but cannot be released. This is not the same as 'Pending' (which means your application is still being reviewed). 'Bank Details Pending' is a payment block, not an application review block. You must fix it before the payment batch closes for the month.
tips: Check your status on srd.sassa.gov.za first — if it says 'Approved' + 'Bank Details Pending', this guide applies.
The payment batch runs in the last week of each month — fix this before the 25th to get paid that month.

steps.title: Fix via the Official SRD Portal (Fastest Method)
steps.content: Go to srd.sassa.gov.za on your phone or computer browser. Scroll down to the section that says 'How do I change my banking details?'. Enter your 13-digit South African ID number and click Submit. SASSA will send a secure link via SMS to your registered cellphone number. Click the link, enter your bank name, account number, and branch code. The account must be in your name. Click Submit. You will see a confirmation message. Your banking details are now updated.
tips: Use a personal bank account in your name — SASSA does not pay into third-party accounts.
Double-check your account number before submitting — one wrong digit delays your payment by another month.

steps.title: Fix via the Moya App (No Data Needed)
steps.content: Download the Moya App from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store. Open the app and look for the 'SASSA SRD' section. Select 'Update Banking Details'. Enter your 13-digit ID number. Enter your bank name, account number, and branch code. Submit the update. The Moya App uses free data for SASSA services, so you do not need to buy airtime or data. The Moya App method is often faster than the web portal because it does not require an SMS OTP link.
tips: Use the Moya App or the SRD portal to update banking details — never share your banking PIN anywhere.
If you updated your details on the portal already, do not update again on Moya — it may create a conflict.

steps.title: Fix via the SRD Portal (Recommended, Confirmed Channel)
steps.content: The confirmed way to update banking details is on the official SRD portal at srd.sassa.gov.za. Log in, go to 'Update Banking Details', and submit your bank name, account number, and branch code. SASSA verifies the account against the name on your ID before the next payment batch. The self-service WhatsApp (082 601 0111) and the Moya App route into the same SASSA system if they offer the option, but the portal is the channel SASSA publishes as the official method for banking changes.
tips: The bank account must be registered in your name — SASSA does not pay into third-party accounts.
Take a screenshot of the confirmation message as proof.

steps.title: Call the SASSA Helpline If Nothing Works
steps.content: If you have tried all three methods above and your status still shows 'Bank Details Pending', call the SASSA helpline on 0800 60 10 11. Explain that you have updated your banking details but the status has not changed. The helpline agent may need to escalate your case to a supervisor. Ask for a reference number for your call. If the helpline cannot resolve it, visit your nearest SASSA office in person with your ID document and bank confirmation letter.
tips: The helpline is toll-free — you do not need airtime to call from any South African network.
Call early in the morning (08:00) to avoid long wait times — afternoons are busiest.

faqs.q: How long does it take for 'Bank Details Pending' to change after I update?
faqs.a: It usually takes 3 to 7 working days for SASSA to verify your new banking details. If you updated before the 25th of the month, you should be included in that month's payment batch.

faqs.q: Can I use a Capitec or TymeBank account for SASSA?
faqs.a: Yes. SASSA pays into all major South African banks including Capitec, FNB, Standard Bank, Nedbank, Absa, TymeBank, Bank Zero, and Discovery Bank. The account must be registered in your name.

faqs.q: What if I updated my details but still did not receive payment?
faqs.a: If your status changed from 'Bank Details Pending' to 'Approved' but you still have not received money, the payment may have been processed in the next batch. Check your status again after the next payment window (last week of the month).

faqs.q: Can I collect my grant at Pick n Pay instead while fixing my bank details?
faqs.a: No. 'Bank Details Pending' means SASSA does not have valid payment information at all. You must first update your banking details. Once updated, you can switch your payment method to Cash Send on the SRD portal for future months.

title: SASSA Biometric Verification Not Working? 7 Common Fixes for 2026
description: Your SASSA biometric (eKYC) verification keeps failing? Fix liveness detection errors, link expiry issues, camera problems, and clear your 'Self-Correction Required' status.
imageAlt: Smartphone showing facial recognition verification screen

steps.title: Why Your Biometric Verification Is Failing
steps.content: SASSA's biometric (eKYC) system uses facial recognition to verify your identity against the Department of Home Affairs database. When it fails, the most common causes are: poor lighting creating shadows on your face, a dirty or smudged phone camera lens, slow internet causing the upload to time out, the SMS verification link has expired (links typically expire within 72 hours), or you are using an old photo instead of a live selfie. The system uses 'liveness detection' — it can tell if you are holding a photo or video up to the camera.
tips: Most biometric failures are caused by lighting or camera issues — fix these first.
The system does NOT store your photo — it only compares it to Home Affairs records and discards it.

steps.title: Fix 1: Improve Your Lighting and Background
steps.content: Good lighting is the single most important factor for successful biometric verification. Sit facing a window during daylight hours — natural light gives the best result. Avoid having a bright light or window behind you (backlighting creates dark shadows on your face). Use a plain, light-coloured wall as your background. Remove hats, sunglasses, and masks. If you wear prescription glasses, keep them on — the system is designed to work with glasses.
tips: Natural daylight from a window is better than room lighting.
If you must do it at night, sit under a bright overhead light facing directly toward you.

steps.title: Fix 2: Clean Your Phone Camera Lens
steps.content: A smudged camera lens is one of the most overlooked causes of biometric failure. Wipe your phone's front camera (selfie camera) with a clean, dry cloth. Many people do not realise their camera lens has fingerprints, dust, or grease on it. After cleaning, test the camera by taking a normal selfie — if it looks clear, the lens is clean enough for biometric verification.
tips: Use a microfiber cloth if available — tissue paper can leave fibers on the lens.
Remove your phone case — some cases partially cover or smudge the camera lens.

steps.title: Fix 3: Use a Strong Internet Connection
steps.content: The biometric verification process uploads a photo to SASSA's servers. If your internet connection is weak, the upload may time out or fail silently. Switch from mobile data to WiFi if available. If you must use mobile data, move to an area with strong signal (preferably 4G or 5G). Do not move around during the verification process — stay still until you see the confirmation screen.
tips: If you have low signal, try going outside or near a window.
Free SASSA services on the Moya App do not cover biometric uploads — you need your own data for this.

steps.title: Fix 4: Request a New Verification Link
steps.content: SASSA's biometric verification links expire within 72 hours. If your link has expired, you will see 'Link Expired' or 'Session Timeout' when you click it. To get a new link, log into the SRD portal at srd.sassa.gov.za. If your status shows 'Biometric Pending' or 'Self-Correction Required', the system should generate a new link within 24 to 48 hours. If it does not, call the SASSA helpline at 0800 60 10 11 and ask them to resend the biometric link.
tips: Complete the verification as soon as you receive the SMS — do not wait.
The SMS link is unique to you — do not share it with anyone.

steps.title: Fix 5: Complete Liveness Detection Correctly
steps.content: The system uses 'liveness detection' to confirm you are a real person, not a photo or video. When prompted: blink both eyes naturally (do not squint), turn your head slowly left and right as instructed, and keep your face centred in the on-screen oval guide. If you fail the liveness check, the system will let you try again — usually up to 3 attempts. After 3 failures, you must request a new link.
tips: Move your head slowly — fast movements confuse the liveness detection AI.
Look directly at the camera, not at the screen showing your own face.

steps.title: Fix 6: Visit a SASSA Office as Last Resort
steps.content: If you have tried all the fixes above and the biometric verification still fails, visit your nearest SASSA office in person. Bring your ID document. Explain that you are unable to complete the online biometric verification. The SASSA officer will verify your identity manually using your fingerprints or by comparing your ID photo to your face. This takes longer, but in-person manual verification successfully resolves most cases.
tips: Go early in the morning (before 08:00) to avoid long queues.
If you cannot travel due to disability or illness, call 0800 60 10 11 to request a home visit.

steps.title: What Is SASSA Beneficiary Biometric Enrolment?
steps.content:
Beneficiary Biometric Enrolment is SASSA's programme to capture your fingerprints or a facial scan as an identity check before a grant is approved or continued. It is different from the online eKYC selfie above: enrolment is done in person at a SASSA office, while eKYC is the online facial check some beneficiaries are asked to complete.

When it applies: compulsory biometric enrolment for new applicants started in September 2025, and face-to-face biometric verification was fully rolled out from 1 September 2026. The online system is being upgraded, with the online social grant system expected to go live by the end of November 2026 (Portfolio Committee on Social Development, 17 September 2026).

What to bring: your original 13-digit barcode ID (Smart ID card or green ID book), and any documents SASSA asked for in your review or application notice. The officer captures your fingerprints or a facial scan and updates your record.

What it does not do: SASSA states that biometric enrolment does not delay or stop a grant, except where your identity cannot be confirmed or fraud is detected. Between September 2025 and March 2026 SASSA biometrically verified 997,379 beneficiaries (Parliamentary reply NW1941, 18 May 2026).
tips: Biometric enrolment is in person at a SASSA office — the online eKYC selfie is a separate step.
Bring your original ID: a photocopy cannot be used for a fingerprint or facial scan.
If online facial verification keeps failing at home, you can complete the biometric step with fingerprints at your nearest office.

faqs.q: What is SASSA Beneficiary Biometric Enrolment?
faqs.a: It is SASSA's identity check where your fingerprints or a facial scan are captured before a grant is approved or continued. It is done in person at a SASSA office and applies to new applicants (since September 2025) and to beneficiaries asked to verify. SASSA says it does not delay or stop a grant unless your identity cannot be confirmed or fraud is detected.

faqs.q: How many times can I retry the biometric verification?
faqs.a: You typically get 3 attempts per verification link. After 3 failures, the link expires and you must request a new one via the SRD portal or by calling SASSA.

faqs.q: Will my biometric data be stored by SASSA?
faqs.a: SASSA states that facial recognition data is compared against Home Affairs records and then discarded. It is not stored permanently. The process complies with POPIA (South Africa's data protection law).

faqs.q: What does 'Self-Correction Required' mean on my status?
faqs.a: This means your biometric verification failed or the link expired. You need to complete the biometric process before your application can proceed to approval. Follow the steps in this guide to fix it.

faqs.q: Can I use my ID photo instead of taking a selfie?
faqs.a: No. The system requires a live selfie for 'liveness detection'. Taking a photo of your ID or a printed photo will be detected as fraud and your verification will fail.

title: How to Work While Receiving the R370 SRD Grant (Legal Rules & the R624 Income Check)
description: You can work and still qualify for the SRD R370 grant — as long as your total monthly deposits stay below R624. Learn how SASSA's income check works, which earnings count, and how to appeal if you are declined.
imageAlt: Person selling vegetables at a roadside stall in South Africa

steps.title: The R624 Rule: How SASSA's Income Check Works
steps.content: SASSA does not say you cannot work. The R370 SRD is for people aged 18 to 59 who are unemployed or earn income below R624 per month. When SASSA checks your eligibility, it uses bank account data to look at the total deposited into accounts linked to your ID number in a month. If that total reaches R625 or more, your SRD status can change to 'Declined' for that month. The R624 check is a total-deposits check, not just a salary check. A R300 deposit from a customer plus R400 from a once-off sale equals R700 — over the limit. Small amounts from a family member, a stokvel payout, or an eWallet transfer can also count, so keep a record of every deposit.
tips: Open a separate bank account for your grant payments only — never let business money go into that account.
If your total deposits for a month stay below R624, your deposits should not affect your eligibility.

steps.title: Cash-Based Micro-Businesses That Work Alongside SRD
steps.content: A cash-in-hand business is a common way to earn extra income while keeping your monthly deposits below R624. The moment cash earnings are deposited into a bank account, they become deposits that count toward the R624 total. Options that often work on a cash basis include selling vegetables or cooked food at a taxi rank, offering domestic work paid in cash, braiding hair or doing nails from home, buying and selling second-hand clothing, offering tutoring or homework help, and doing small handyman jobs. If a customer wants to pay via eWallet or bank transfer, remember that transfer will land in a bank account and count toward your deposits for that month.
tips: Keeping earnings in cash means no new bank deposit is created — but you must still answer SASSA honestly when you apply or appeal.
Keep your business small and cash-based — opening a business bank account means every deposit will count toward the R624 total.

steps.title: Using the Moya App for SASSA Tasks and Small Earnings
steps.content: The Moya App is a free, data-free messaging platform that offers SASSA SRD services such as status checks, banking detail updates, and appeals. Moya also lets you earn airtime, data, or MoyaPoints by completing small tasks and surveys. Because these earnings are paid out as airtime, data, or app credits rather than a bank deposit, they do not create a deposit that counts toward the R624 total. Always download the Moya App from the official Google Play or Apple App Store. Note that Moya's SASSA services do not cover biometric uploads — you need your own data for that.
tips: MoyaPoints and airtime earnings are not bank deposits, so they do not count toward the R624 deposit total.
Use Moya for SASSA status checks and banking updates — it is free of data charges for those services.

steps.title: What Happens If You Deposit Cash into Your Bank Account
steps.content: Once you deposit cash into a bank account linked to your ID number, that amount counts toward your monthly deposit total. A cash deposit of R500 plus a grant payment of R370 equals R870 in deposits — well over the R624 limit. The eligibility check is done per month, so a month where your total deposits stay below R624 may still qualify. If you need to save cash earnings, keeping them outside the bank means no deposit is created, but you must still be honest about your income in your application.
tips: If your monthly deposits including your grant stay below R624, your deposits should not affect your eligibility for that month.
R370 grant + R250 deposit = R620 — under the limit. R370 + R300 = R670 — over the limit.

steps.title: Online and App Earnings: What Counts and What You Must Declare
steps.content: Some online platforms pay out in airtime, vouchers, or app credits that never enter a South African bank account. Because the R624 check is based on bank deposits, those credits do not appear in the deposit check. However, they are still income: you must answer SASSA honestly when you apply or appeal, and SASSA may cross-check other records such as payroll, UIF, SARS, or Home Affairs data. If you are paid into PayPal or a crypto wallet, that money only counts toward the R624 deposit check when it is transferred into a bank account linked to your ID number.
tips: Income paid into PayPal or a crypto wallet only becomes a deposit when you move it into a South African bank account linked to your ID.
Keep total monthly deposits below R624 and keep proof of your income to support an appeal.

steps.title: How to Appeal If Your SRD Was Declined
steps.content: If SASSA declined your grant because your deposits exceeded R624, you can appeal. Go to srd-appeals.dsd.gov.za and select the declined month. Choose the reason that matches your situation (such as 'Income Source Detected'), and in your explanation describe your circumstances honestly, for example: 'I run a small informal business selling vegetables. The deposit of RXXX was from a once-off sale, not a salary. My income for the month was still below R624.' Write truthfully — a false appeal is more likely to be rejected. If your total deposits genuinely exceeded R624, the appeal may not succeed. If you were close to the limit or the decline was due to a misunderstanding, the Independent Tribunal may rule in your favour. Submit your appeal within 90 days of the decline.
tips: Every declined month must be appealed separately within 90 days.
Keep bank statements and proof of income so you can support your appeal with evidence.

faqs.q: Is it legal to work while receiving the SRD grant?
faqs.a: Yes. The R370 SRD is for people aged 18 to 59 who are unemployed or earn income below R624 per month. You may work and still qualify, as long as your monthly income stays under the threshold. The rule controls income, not whether you work at all.

faqs.q: What counts toward the R624 limit?
faqs.a: Any money deposited into a bank account linked to your ID number — salaries, business earnings, cash you deposit yourself, eWallet transfers, and other deposits. If your total deposits in a month reach R625 or more, you may lose that month's payment.

faqs.q: Can I run a spaza shop and still get SRD?
faqs.a: Yes, if you keep your total monthly bank deposits under R624. If you deposit spaza shop earnings into a bank account, those deposits count as income and may cause a decline for that month.

faqs.q: Does SASSA check Moya App earnings?
faqs.a: Moya pays out in airtime, data, or MoyaPoints rather than a bank deposit, so those credits do not create a deposit that SASSA counts toward the R624 total. They are still income, so answer SASSA honestly and keep your total income within the allowed limits.

faqs.q: Can I use PayPal for freelance work while on SRD?
faqs.a: Money kept in a PayPal account is not a deposit into a South African bank account, so it does not appear in the R624 deposit check — but it is still income. If you transfer it into a bank account linked to your ID, it counts as a deposit. Always answer SASSA honestly.

title: How to Fix 'Income Source Detected' SASSA Decline: Step-by-Step ITSAA Appeal Guide
description: Your SRD was declined because SASSA says they detected 'alternative income'. Most of the time this is a mistake — a family transfer, stokvel payout, or once-off deposit. Here is exactly how to appeal to the Independent Tribunal and get your back pay.
imageAlt: Paper document with a stamp reading 'Appeal'

steps.title: Understand Why You Got 'Income Source Detected'
steps.content: When SASSA declines your SRD and shows 'Income Source Detected', it means their automated system found deposits in your bank accounts that pushed your total monthly deposits over R624. This is the most common decline reason in 2026 — the system scans all bank accounts linked to your ID number. It counts every deposit: salary, family gift, stokvel payout, e-wallet transfer, refund, even money you transferred from your own savings account. The system does not know the difference between a salary and a gift from your mother. If that total exceeds R624, you are declined. The good news: this is the most winnable appeal category because many deposits are not actually 'income'.
tips: Check your bank statements for the declined month to identify what deposit triggered the flag.
The most common false positives: family support transfers, stokvel payouts, and retailer refunds.

steps.title: Gather Your Evidence Before You Appeal
steps.content: Before opening the ITSAA portal, gather your evidence. You will need: your bank statement for the declined month showing the specific deposit, proof that the deposit was not income (a letter from your stokvel, a family member's affidavit saying they sent you money as a gift, or a receipt showing the deposit was a refund), your 13-digit ID number, and your original SRD application reference number if you have it. The quality of your evidence determines whether you win. A vague explanation like 'that money was not income' is weaker than 'I have attached a bank statement and an affidavit from my sister confirming she sent me R500 for my child's school fees.' Take screenshots of relevant SMS or WhatsApp conversations showing the purpose of the transfer.
tips: Request a free bank statement from your bank's app or visit a branch — most give 3 months free.
If you know who sent you the money, ask them to write a brief letter explaining the purpose.

steps.title: Access the ITSAA Appeals Portal
steps.content: Go to srd-appeals.dsd.gov.za on your phone or computer. This is the official Independent Tribunal for Social Assistance Appeals website. On the homepage, enter your 13-digit SA ID number. Select the month that was declined from the dropdown. Click Submit. The system will look up your application and show your decline reason. If you see multiple declined months, you must submit a separate appeal for each month — one appeal per month, one month at a time.
tips: Bookmark srd-appeals.dsd.gov.za — it is the only legitimate appeals portal.
If the portal does not load, try Chrome — some older browsers have compatibility issues.

steps.title: Write Your Appeal Explanation
steps.content: This is the most important step. The form has a text box where you explain why the deposit should not count as income. Write clearly and factually. A good explanation: 'On 15 March 2026, my sister sent me R500 via eWallet for my child's school uniform. This was a once-off family gift, not a salary or regular income. My total bank deposits for March were R500 plus my SRD grant of R370, totalling R870. I did not receive any salary, UIF, or other income. I have attached my bank statement and an affidavit from my sister as proof.' Be specific about dates, amounts, and the source. If you attached documents, mention them. If the deposit was a stokvel payout, explain it was your own savings being returned.
tips: Do not lie — ITSAA can request bank statements from SASSA to verify your claims.
Keep your explanation between 3 to 6 sentences — tribunal members read hundreds per day.

steps.title: Upload Supporting Documents
steps.content: The ITSAA portal allows document uploads (PDF, JPG, PNG — max 5MB per file). Upload your bank statement highlighting the specific deposit, any supporting letters or affidavits, and any SMS or WhatsApp screenshots. If you cannot upload documents from your phone, you can still submit the appeal without attachments — just be very specific in your written explanation. The tribunal may contact you for documents later. Review everything before clicking Submit. Once submitted, you cannot edit your appeal.
tips: Take clear photos with good lighting — blurry documents are not accepted as evidence.
Use a scanning app like CamScanner if you do not have a scanner.

steps.title: Track Your Appeal Status
steps.content: After submitting, you will receive an acknowledgment SMS from ITSAA within 1 to 3 working days. The SMS includes your appeal reference number — write it down. Check your status anytime at srd-appeals.dsd.gov.za. Statuses: 'Appeal Pending' (under review), 'Appeal Approved' (you won), 'Appeal Declined' (tribunal agreed with SASSA). Most appeals take 60 to 90 days, but simple cases with clear evidence can be resolved in 30 days. If approved, SASSA will pay you within 7 to 14 working days.
tips: Check your appeal status once per week — not daily.
If your appeal exceeds 90 days with no decision, call 0800 60 10 11 and ask for a status update.

steps.title: What to Do If Your Appeal Is Declined
steps.content: If ITSAA declines your appeal, first read the reason carefully. If you have new evidence, submit a fresh appeal for the same month with the new evidence. If your appeal was declined because your deposits genuinely exceeded R624, focus on keeping future months under the limit. You can request reasons in writing from ITSAA by calling 0800 60 10 11. If you believe the system is fundamentally wrong, escalate to the Department of Social Development at 012 312 7726 or visit your nearest SASSA office with your evidence.
tips: A declined appeal does not affect future months — you can still be approved for the next month.
Legal Aid SA (0800 110 110) can assist if you want to challenge the decision further.

faqs.q: How long does an 'Income Source Detected' appeal take?
faqs.a: Most appeals are decided within 60 to 90 days. Simple cases with clear evidence can be approved in 30 days. During peak periods, the tribunal may take the full 90 days.

faqs.q: Can I appeal if the deposit was actually my salary?
faqs.a: If you received a salary that pushed you over R624, you genuinely exceeded the threshold and the appeal is unlikely to succeed. However, if the income was once-off, mention this — the tribunal has discretion.

faqs.q: Can I appeal through Moya App or WhatsApp?
faqs.a: Yes, both methods work. However, they do not allow document uploads. For an 'Income Source Detected' appeal where evidence matters, use the ITSAA website.

title: SASSA Bulk Means Test: Why SASSA Checks Your Bank Accounts and How to Respond
description: SASSA uses the bulk means test to check if beneficiaries have undisclosed income flowing into bank accounts they did not declare. Learn what triggers it, how to respond, and what happens if you ignore it.

steps.title: What Is the SASSA Bulk Means Test?
steps.content: The bulk means test is an automated system SASSA uses to cross-check beneficiary information against other government and financial databases. Unlike the standard means test (which you complete when you apply for a grant), the bulk means test runs silently in the background every month. SASSA compares your declared income against data from SARS, banks, UIF, NSFAS, the Department of Home Affairs, and the Payments Association of South Africa (PASA). If the system finds deposits in bank accounts you did not declare, or income that exceeds the threshold for your grant type, you may be flagged for review. In the May 2025 statement, SASSA confirmed they are targeting 'beneficiaries identified through the bulk means test process, to check if they have some income that flows into other bank accounts that they did not disclose to SASSA.' This is not a new rule — it is an existing process that SASSA has strengthened.
tips: The bulk means test runs automatically — you do not need to do anything unless SASSA contacts you.
SASSA can see all bank accounts linked to your ID number, not just the one you declared.

steps.title: Why SASSA Checks Your Bank Accounts
steps.content: SASSA's mandate is to pay grants only to people who genuinely qualify. The bulk means test ensures that beneficiaries who have income from other sources are not receiving grants they are not entitled to. The system specifically looks for: bank accounts that receive regular deposits not declared in your application, income from part-time or informal work, rental income, pension income from other sources (like a private pension or retirement annuity), and any deposits that push your total monthly income over the threshold for your grant type. For the SRD R370 grant, the threshold is R624 per month total deposits. For permanent grants like Old Age, the income threshold is much higher (R9,350/month for a single person). The system does not look at your spending — only deposits. SASSA cannot see what you spend your money on, only what comes into your accounts.
tips: A single deposit of R625 or more in a month can trigger an SRD decline — even if it is a gift.
SASSA does not check cash in your home or money held outside the banking system.

steps.title: Who Gets Flagged by the Bulk Means Test?
steps.content: Not everyone is flagged. The bulk means test targets specific beneficiary groups. In the May 2025 statement, SASSA identified two groups: (1) Beneficiaries using alternative forms of identification — people who receive grants using documents other than the standard 13-digit South African ID number, such as refugee permits, asylum seeker documents, or special permits (ZEP/LEP). (2) Beneficiaries flagged by the bulk means test process — those whose bank accounts show deposits that were not declared in their grant application. You may also be flagged if you recently received a large once-off deposit, your bank account shows regular deposits from multiple sources, or SARS records show income you did not declare to SASSA. Being flagged does not automatically mean your grant stops. It means SASSA wants to verify your information.
tips: Being flagged does not mean you did something wrong — it may be a system error or a once-off deposit.
If you are flagged, SASSA will contact you directly — do not respond to anyone who contacts you first claiming to be SASSA.

steps.title: What to Do If SASSA Flags You
steps.content: If the bulk means test identifies a discrepancy, SASSA will contact you through official channels — either by SMS, letter, or a call from a SASSA office. They will ask you to visit your nearest SASSA office to update your information. What to do: (1) Verify the contact is really from SASSA — only respond to messages from official SASSA sources. Visit your nearest SASSA office in person rather than calling a number in an SMS, which could be a scam. (2) Bring your ID document and any documents showing your income sources — bank statements, payslips, affidavits explaining deposits. (3) Be honest about your financial situation — if you have income you did not declare, tell the SASSA officer. They will calculate whether you still qualify for the grant. (4) If the discrepancy was a mistake (e.g., a family member sent you money once), explain this and provide supporting documents.
tips: Never give your banking PIN, SASSA card PIN, or passwords to anyone who contacts you.
If you are unsure whether the contact is legitimate, call the SASSA helpline first: 0800 60 10 11.

steps.title: What Happens If You Ignore the Flag?
steps.content: If SASSA contacts you about a bulk means test flag and you do not respond, your grant may be suspended or declined. SASSA cannot verify your eligibility without your cooperation. If your grant is suspended, you will need to visit a SASSA office to have it reinstated. In serious cases where SASSA finds clear evidence of fraud (such as undeclared employment), you may be required to repay grants you received while not entitled. However, honest mistakes — like a once-off gift pushing you over the threshold — do not result in penalties. You simply lose the grant for that month or have it adjusted going forward. The key is to respond promptly when SASSA contacts you.
tips: Ignoring SASSA does not make the issue go away — it makes it worse.
If you are too ill or disabled to visit a SASSA office, call 0800 60 10 11 to arrange a home visit.

steps.title: Difference Between Bulk Means Test and Standard Means Test
steps.content: Many beneficiaries confuse the bulk means test with the standard means test. The standard means test is the assessment you complete when you first apply for a grant — you declare your income, assets, and household situation. The bulk means test is a separate, ongoing verification process that SASSA runs after your grant is approved. Key differences: The standard means test is a one-time assessment (though it can be reviewed). The bulk means test runs monthly for SRD grants and periodically for permanent grants. The standard means test relies on what you declare. The bulk means test cross-checks your declaration against third-party data from SARS, banks, and other sources. The standard means test requires you to provide documents. The bulk means test runs automatically without any input from you.
tips: Always declare all your income honestly when applying — the bulk means test will catch undeclared income.
If your financial situation changes (you get a job, inherit money, or receive UIF), update your details with SASSA proactively.

steps.title: Standard Means Test: Income and Asset Thresholds
steps.content:
The standard means test is the assessment SASSA uses for permanent grants. It checks your income and your assets against set limits (thresholds) for each grant. As of 2026 the income thresholds for the main grants are:
  • Old Age Grant: R9,350 per month for a single person, or R18,700 combined for a married couple.
  • Disability Grant: R9,350 per month for a single person, or R18,700 combined for a married couple.
  • Child Support Grant: R5,800 per month for a single caregiver, or R11,600 combined for a married couple.
The asset thresholds for the Old Age and Disability Grants are R1,584,000 for a single person and R3,168,000 for a married couple. Assets include property (other than the home you live in), vehicles, and investments. The Child Support Grant does not have an asset test. Your spouse's income and assets may also be considered. The SRD R370 grant uses a different, lower income check of R624 per month based on bank deposits.
tips: Income includes salaries, wages, pensions, and any other regular payments you receive.
The value of the home you live in is not included in the asset test.
The thresholds above are the 2026 figures — SASSA reviews them each year and they can change.

faqs.q: Can SASSA see all my bank accounts?
faqs.a: Yes, SASSA can see all bank accounts linked to your ID number through the Payments Association of South Africa (PASA) verification system. This includes accounts you may not have declared in your grant application.

faqs.q: Will my grant stop if SASSA finds undeclared income?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. If the undeclared income is small or was a once-off mistake, SASSA may adjust your grant or require you to repay the overpayment for specific months. If the income shows you no longer qualify, your grant may be canceled.

faqs.q: How do I know if the bulk means test flagged me?
faqs.a: SASSA will contact you directly through official channels (SMS from a SASSA short code, a letter from your local SASSA office, or a call from a SASSA official). You will be asked to visit a SASSA office to update your information.

faqs.q: Can I check if the bulk means test has flagged me online?
faqs.a: Not directly. The bulk means test flag does not appear as a status on the SRD portal. You will only know you were flagged if SASSA contacts you. However, if your grant status suddenly changes from 'Approved' to 'Pending' or 'Declined' without explanation, it may be related to a bulk means test flag.

title: SASSA Grants with Alternative ID: Guide for Refugees, Asylum Seekers & Special Permit Holders
description: If you use a refugee permit, asylum seeker document, or special permit (ZEP/LEP) instead of a 13-digit SA ID, this guide explains how to apply for grants, what documents you need, and how the verification process affects you.

steps.title: Who Needs to Use Alternative ID for SASSA Grants?
steps.content: Most SASSA grant applicants use their 13-digit South African ID number. But some beneficiaries receive grants using alternative forms of identification. These include: refugees with valid refugee status recognised by the Department of Home Affairs, asylum seekers with valid permits under the Refugees Act, special permit holders under the Zimbabwe Exemption Permit (ZEP) or Lesotho Exemption Permit (LEP), and certain permanent residents whose ID documents are not the standard 13-digit format. In May 2025, SASSA confirmed they are specifically targeting beneficiaries who use 'alternative forms of identification other than the standard 13-digit South African identity number' as part of their verification process. These beneficiaries are being asked to visit SASSA offices to update their information.
tips: If you are a South African citizen with a 13-digit ID number, the alternative ID verification does not apply to you.
Foreign nationals with valid permits can and do receive SASSA grants — the verification is part of standard integrity checks.

steps.title: Which SASSA Grants Can Foreign Nationals Apply For?
steps.content: Not all SASSA grants are available to foreign nationals. The SRD R370 grant is the most commonly accessed grant for refugees, asylum seekers, and special permit holders, provided they meet the income criteria (monthly income under R624). The Child Support Grant may be available to refugees and permanent residents who meet the means test. The Old Age Grant and Disability Grant are generally restricted to South African citizens and permanent residents. If you are a refugee or asylum seeker, you must have your status recognised by the Department of Home Affairs. A pending asylum application does not qualify you for grants. Your permit must be valid and not expired.
tips: You cannot apply for a SASSA grant if your permit has expired — renew it with Home Affairs first.
The SRD grant is the most accessible option for foreign nationals — apply online at srd.sassa.gov.za.

steps.title: What Documents Do You Need?
steps.content: When applying for a SASSA grant with alternative ID, you need: (1) Your valid permit or document — refugee ID, asylum seeker permit, or special permit (ZEP/LEP). The document must be original and not expired. (2) Your file number or permit number as issued by the Department of Home Affairs. (3) Proof of residence in South Africa — a utility bill, lease agreement, or affidavit from your landlord. (4) A registered cellphone number in your name (must be RICA-compliant). (5) Proof of income or an affidavit explaining your financial situation. For the SRD grant, you apply online at srd.sassa.gov.za using your permit number instead of a 13-digit SA ID. If you are applying for a permanent grant, you must visit a SASSA office in person.
tips: Make copies of all your documents before visiting a SASSA office — keep originals safe.
If your permit is under renewal, get a receipt from Home Affairs as proof that renewal is in progress.

steps.title: The Verification Process for Alternative ID Beneficiaries
steps.content: In the May 2025 statement, SASSA confirmed they are targeting beneficiaries using alternative ID for verification. This is what happens: (1) SASSA identifies beneficiaries whose grants are linked to non-13-digit ID numbers. (2) These beneficiaries are contacted directly by SASSA — through official SMS or letter — and asked to visit a SASSA office. (3) At the office, a SASSA officer reviews your original permit or ID document. (4) The officer checks that your permit is valid and matches the details in the SASSA system. (5) You may be asked to provide updated contact information and proof of residence. (6) Your information is updated in the system and your grant continues as normal. This verification is standard — it does not mean your grant is at risk. It is simply a data quality check to ensure SASSA has accurate records.
tips: Only respond to verification requests that come from official SASSA channels — visit a SASSA office in person.
The verification is free — no one should ask you to pay to update your information.

steps.title: What Happens If You Do Not Respond to the Verification?
steps.content: If SASSA asks you to verify your alternative ID information and you do not respond, your grant may be suspended. SASSA cannot continue paying a grant without confirming that the beneficiary's documents are still valid. If your grant is suspended, you must visit a SASSA office with your valid permit to have it reinstated. If your permit has expired, you must renew it with the Department of Home Affairs first. Once you present a valid permit, your grant will be reinstated and you will receive back pay from the date of suspension.
tips: Check your permit expiry date regularly — an expired permit will cause your grant to be suspended.
Start the renewal process with Home Affairs at least 3 months before your permit expires.

steps.title: Scam Warning for Foreign National Beneficiaries
steps.content: Scammers specifically target foreign national beneficiaries because they may be less familiar with SASSA processes. Remember: SASSA will never ask for your banking PIN or password. No one from SASSA will visit your home to 'verify' your documents — you must go to a SASSA office. No payment is required for any verification or update process. Only trust communications from official channels: calls from 0800 60 10 11, SMS from SASSA short codes, or letters from your local SASSA office. If someone contacts you claiming to be from SASSA and asks for money or personal banking details, report them to the SASSA fraud hotline.
tips: Never share your permit number or banking details with anyone who contacts you on WhatsApp or Facebook.
If you are unsure about a message, call the SASSA helpline on 0800 60 10 11 before taking any action.

faqs.q: Can I apply for a SASSA grant if my asylum seeker permit is still pending?
faqs.a: No. You need a valid refugee status or asylum seeker permit recognised by the Department of Home Affairs. A pending application does not qualify.

faqs.q: My ZEP permit expired — can I still receive my grant?
faqs.a: No. Your grant will be suspended if your permit expires. You must renew your permit with Home Affairs and present the new permit at a SASSA office to have your grant reinstated.

faqs.q: Can I use my foreign passport to apply for a SASSA grant?
faqs.a: No. SASSA requires a South African-issued permit or ID document. A foreign passport alone is not accepted. You need a valid refugee, asylum seeker, or special permit issued by the Department of Home Affairs.

faqs.q: Will the verification process affect my grant amount?
faqs.a: No. The verification is to confirm your identity and permit validity, not to reassess your grant amount. Your grant amount stays the same unless your financial situation has changed.

title: SASSA Grant Reviews & Verification Process (Complete Guide)
description: Complete guide to SASSA grant reviews and verification for 2026/27. If you received an SMS or letter asking you to visit a SASSA office, here is exactly what will happen, what documents to bring, and what to do if you miss your appointment.

steps.title: Why SASSA Is Doing Verification
steps.content:
SASSA conducts targeted verification to make sure that grant payments go to the right people. It is part of SASSA's ongoing integrity measures and is aimed at beneficiaries using alternative forms of identification (non-13-digit SA ID numbers) and beneficiaries flagged by data cross-checks — for example when a bank account shows deposits that were not declared. The goal is not to stop grants — it is to make sure the information SASSA has on file is accurate. SASSA is required by law to verify beneficiary information regularly.

October 2026 update: In its 2025/26 audit, the Auditor-General told Parliament that SASSA paid over R1.33 billion to ineligible beneficiaries (down from R2.3 billion the year before), including payments made after death and to government employees earning above the threshold. SASSA defended its reviews in a statement on 9 October 2026, saying the checks are integrity controls and are not designed to terminate grants arbitrarily. SASSA also clarified the difference between an assessment and a review: a review is an administrative control to confirm you still qualify, and it does not automatically mean your grant is cancelled. If your information is correct, the process is quick and your grant continues unchanged. Read the full SASSA statement in our grant-controls update.
tips: This verification is routine — it does not mean you are accused of fraud.
SASSA will contact you directly — do not respond to unsolicited calls or messages.

steps.title: The 2026/27 Review Wave: What Is Happening Now
steps.content:
SASSA is reviewing a large number of grants during the 2026/27 financial year. Here are the confirmed facts, with official sources:

  • More than 350,000 beneficiaries are targeted for review in 2026/27 (Parliamentary reply NW4094, 17 September 2026).
  • In 2025/26, 169,049 beneficiaries received a notice but did not present themselves, and their grants lapsed, were cancelled or terminated. Of those, 31,759 later presented, were found to still qualify, and had their grants restored (Parliamentary reply NW4450, 17 September 2026).
  • In the first quarter of 2026/27, SASSA reviewed 105,508 grants (Parliamentary reply NW4444, 17 September 2026).
  • Across the first two quarters, about 259,000 reviews were initiated — including about 104,000 Child Support Grants and 102,000 Older Persons Grants — with about 201,000 beneficiaries responding and roughly 60,000 suspension notices issued (Portfolio Committee on Social Development, 17 September 2026).
  • SASSA has said reviews will pause temporarily in November and December 2026, and biometric verification (face to face) was rolled out from 1 September 2026.

Key point: if you receive a review notice, do not ignore it. Most beneficiaries who attend and still qualify keep their grant, and grants can be restored even after they lapse.
tips: The figures change as the financial year progresses — always confirm the current position with SASSA on 0800 60 10 11.
A review notice is not an accusation of fraud. It is a routine eligibility check.

steps.title: How Will You Know If You Are Selected?
steps.content:
If you are selected for verification or a grant review, SASSA will contact you through official channels. This may be: an SMS from a SASSA-registered short code asking you to visit your nearest SASSA office, a formal letter delivered to your address on SASSA letterhead, or a phone call from your local SASSA office.

Review SMS Notifications: SASSA sends SMS messages to beneficiaries selected for review before the payment cycle begins. A genuine review SMS will tell you that your grant has been flagged for review, instruct you to visit a SASSA office, and include the documents you need to bring. Genuine SASSA SMS messages come from registered short codes — not regular cellphone numbers or WhatsApp. They will never ask for your banking PIN, SASSA card PIN, or passwords. If you receive a message asking for this information, it is a scam. Check your phone messages carefully — if your contact details are outdated, you may miss the notification and only discover you are under review when your payment does not arrive on the normal day.

The communication will tell you which documents to bring and which office to visit. Important: SASSA will never ask for your banking PIN, SASSA card PIN, or passwords over the phone or SMS. If someone contacts you asking for this information, it is a scam. If you are unsure whether the contact is real, call the SASSA helpline on 0800 60 10 11 to verify before taking any action.
tips: SASSA does not have the capacity to call every beneficiary — if you are selected, the contact will be official and verifiable.
If you receive an SMS with a link to click, check the URL carefully — real SASSA links end in .gov.za.
Keep your cellphone number updated — if you changed your number recently, visit SASSA to update it immediately.

steps.title: Review Appointments: What to Expect
steps.content:
When SASSA contacts you for a review, they will ask you to visit your nearest SASSA office for an appointment. Here is what you need to know:

How Appointments Work: Review appointments are not pre-scheduled with a specific time. You visit the SASSA office during working hours (08:00 to 15:00, Monday to Friday), take a queue ticket, and wait for your number to be called. There is no online booking system for review appointments.

What Happens During the Appointment: The SASSA officer will review your documents, compare them against the information in the SASSA system, update your contact details and income declaration as needed, and confirm whether your information is correct. The actual document review takes 15 to 30 minutes, not including waiting time.

How to Reschedule: If you cannot attend on the date SMSsed to you, call the SASSA helpline on 0800 60 10 11 to reschedule. Do not simply skip the appointment — failing to attend may result in suspension. If you are too ill or disabled to visit an office, request a home visit when you call.

What If You Missed the SMS? If you lost the SMS or letter asking you to come for a review, go to your nearest SASSA office with your ID document and explain that you received a review request. The officer can look up your record and proceed without the original message.
tips: Go early in the morning (before 08:00) to avoid the longest queues.
Tuesday to Thursday are generally less busy than Monday and Friday.
Bring a pen and water — wait times can be 2 to 3 hours at busy offices.

steps.title: What Documents Must You Bring?
steps.content: When you visit a SASSA office for verification, bring these documents: (1) Your original 13-digit South African ID book or Smart ID card. If you use alternative ID, bring your original refugee permit, asylum seeker document, or special permit. (2) Proof of residence — a utility bill, bank statement, or lease agreement dated within the last 3 months. (3) Your SASSA card (Postbank Black Card or old Gold Card) if you have it. (4) Proof of any income you receive — payslips if employed, pension statements, bank statements showing deposits, or an affidavit if you are unemployed. (5) Any documents SASSA specifically asked for in their message to you. Bring original documents plus photocopies. Some SASSA offices offer copying services, but not all.
tips: Make photocopies of all documents before leaving home — keep originals in a safe folder.
If you were asked to bring a specific document and you do not have it, go anyway and explain — the officer may accept an alternative.

steps.title: What Happens at the SASSA Office?
steps.content: The verification process at the SASSA office is straightforward: (1) Take a queue ticket and wait for your number to be called (bring something to read — wait times can be long). (2) When called, explain to the officer that you are there for a verification appointment. Give them any SMS or letter you received. (3) The officer will review your documents and compare them against the information in the SASSA system. (4) They will update your contact details, ID information, and income declaration as needed. (5) The officer will confirm whether your information is correct and your grant will continue. (6) Ask for a confirmation slip or reference number as proof that you completed the verification. The entire process usually takes 15 to 30 minutes, not including waiting time.
tips: Go early in the morning (before 08:00) to avoid the longest queues.
Bring a pen — you may need to fill out a form.

steps.title: What Happens If You Do Not Attend the Review or Verification?
steps.content:
If SASSA asks you to attend a review or verification and you do not go, your grant can be suspended and later lapsed. SASSA cannot keep paying a grant while verification of your situation is outstanding.

The staged timeline (2026/27):

  • Day 1 to 30: after SASSA notifies you, you have an initial 30 days to submit the information and documents requested.
  • Day 31 to 90: if there is no response, SASSA allows a further 60 days before the grant is suspended — so you have up to 90 days in total from the notice to present yourself (Parliamentary replies NW4094 and NW4444, 17 September 2026).
  • If you still do not respond: the grant is suspended. You then have 30 days from the suspension to apply for restoration (SASSA Grant Booklet 2026).
  • If there is still no response: the grant can be lapsed after one month's notice (Parliamentary reply NW1941, 18 May 2026).

How to reinstate: if you attend after a suspension and SASSA confirms you still qualify, the suspension is lifted and you are back-paid for the period you were suspended. In 2025/26, 31,759 beneficiaries whose grants had lapsed later presented, were found to still qualify, and had their grants restored (Parliamentary reply NW4450, 17 September 2026).

Do not ignore the request or wait for a reminder — the review process pauses in November and December 2026. Even if you think your information is correct, attend the review to confirm it officially. If your grant has been suspended or lapsed, visit your nearest SASSA office with your ID and documents as soon as possible, or call 0800 60 10 11. Read the full SASSA statement in our grant-controls update.
tips: If you cannot attend on the scheduled date, call the SASSA helpline to reschedule — do not just skip it.
If you are too ill or disabled to visit an office, call 0800 60 10 11 to request a home visit.
A suspension can be reversed by completing the review. Even a lapsed grant can be restored if you present yourself later and still qualify.

steps.title: How This Differs from Life Certification
steps.content: Many beneficiaries confuse the verification process with life certification. They are different: Life certification is annual — every beneficiary must confirm they are still alive once every 12 months. The verification process is targeted — only specific beneficiaries are asked to attend, and only when SASSA identifies a data discrepancy. Life certification can be done online, via WhatsApp, or at a SASSA office. The verification process usually requires a physical visit because documents need to be reviewed. Life certification is about confirming you are alive. The verification process is about confirming your financial and identity information is accurate. If you are asked to attend verification, complete it promptly — it is a separate requirement from your annual life certification.
tips: If you complete life certification online, it does not automatically complete the verification process — they are separate.
Ask the SASSA officer whether you also need to complete life certification while you are there.

faqs.q: How long does the SASSA verification process take?
faqs.a: The actual document review takes 15 to 30 minutes. Waiting time at the office depends on how busy it is — go early in the morning (before 08:00) to minimise waiting.

faqs.q: Will my grant stop while I wait for verification?
faqs.a: No. Your grant continues as normal unless your documents show that you no longer qualify. The verification is to confirm your information, not to pause your payments.

faqs.q: Can I send someone else to the verification appointment for me?
faqs.a: No. The verification requires you to attend in person because SASSA needs to see your original documents and compare them to you. If you are too ill or disabled to attend, call 0800 60 10 11 to request a home visit. Alternatively, you can authorise a trusted family member with a signed letter — they must bring their own ID and copies of your documents.

faqs.q: What if I lost the SMS or letter asking me to come for verification?
faqs.a: Go to your nearest SASSA office with your ID document and explain that you received a review request. The officer can look up your record and proceed without the original message.

faqs.q: I received an SMS about a grant review — is it real and what do I do?
faqs.a: Genuine SASSA review SMS messages come from registered short codes and tell you to visit a SASSA office. They never ask for your PIN, OTP, or banking password. If you are unsure, call 0800 60 10 11 to verify. For detailed guidance on identifying real vs fake SMS messages, see our guide on what to do if SASSA asks you to update your information.

faqs.q: Can I reschedule my review appointment?
faqs.a: Yes. If you cannot attend on the date given, call the SASSA helpline on 0800 60 10 11 to reschedule. Do not simply skip the appointment — failing to attend may result in your grant being suspended.

faqs.q: Is a SASSA review the same as a cancellation?
faqs.a: No. A review is an administrative check to confirm that you still qualify. It is not a cancellation, and it does not automatically mean your grant is stopped. SASSA clarified on 9 October 2026 that reviews are integrity controls and are not a programme to terminate grants arbitrarily.

faqs.q: How long do I have to present myself for a SASSA review?
faqs.a: SASSA allows up to 90 days from the date of the notice: an initial 30 days to submit the requested information, and a further 60 days before the grant may be suspended (Parliamentary reply NW4444, 17 September 2026). Do not wait — visit your nearest SASSA office or call 0800 60 10 11 as soon as you receive a notice. Reviews pause in November and December 2026, so attend early.

faqs.q: My grant was suspended or lapsed after a review — can I get it back?
faqs.a: Yes, in many cases. If you present yourself and SASSA confirms you still qualify, the suspension is lifted and you are back-paid for the suspended period. If your grant has already been suspended, apply for restoration within 30 days of the suspension (SASSA Grant Booklet 2026). In 2025/26, 31,759 beneficiaries whose grants had lapsed later presented and had their grants restored (Parliamentary reply NW4450). Visit a SASSA office with your ID and documents as soon as possible.
